p.seg: “Xiàolín.” A man from Wú arrived at the capital.
At a banquet, the host served him làosū.
Not knowing what it was,
he forced himself to eat it.
After returning home, he vomited and fell into exhaustion.
He said to his son,
“Dying together with Cāng people,
I have no regrets;
yet you ought to be careful.”
Lèi Jù seventy-two, Yùlǎn eight hundred fifty-eight.
A man from Tàiyuán lost his home to fire at night.
He carried out his possessions,
and wanted to bring out a bronze spear.
By mistake, he brought out an iron,
which greatly surprised and alarmed him.
He said to his son,
“A strange thing! (Two characters, Lèi Jù cites)
The fire has not yet reached here,
and the spear has already been burned so that its shaft is lost!”
Shū Chāo one hundred thirty-five, Lèi Jù seventy-two, Yùlǎn seven hundred fifty-seven.
Someone (Guǎngjì gives as Wèi man) fell seriously ill at night,
and ordered his servant to drill fire.
That night it was dark and cloudy, and fire could not be obtained,
the urging was urgent, (Guǎngjì: the urging was quite severe)
the servant angrily said,
“Your rebuke is truly unreasonable!
It is now as dark as lacquer—why don’t you shine some fire for me?
I must go seek tools for drilling fire, (Lèi Jù eighty, Yùlǎn eight hundred sixty-nine: only then will it be easy.)” Kǒng Wénjǔ heard and said,
“Rebuking others should be done in their place.” Guǎngjì two hundred fifty-eight.
There was a man who attended a funeral, wishing also to bring something as assistance.
He asked someone, “What sort of thing should I give?”
The other answered, “Money, cloth, grain, silk—whatever you have!”
So he brought a bushel of beans and set it before the bereaved son, saying,
“I have nothing suitable; I offer one bushel of large beans as help.”
The filial son cried, “What shall I do?”
The man thought he was asking about the beans,
and replied, “You can make rice with them!”
The filial son cried again, “Poor!”
The man said, (Guǎngjì: the filial son cried again, ‘Poor and alone, what shall I do?’ The man said)
“If poor, then I should send another bushel.”
Lèi Jù eighty-five, Guǎngjì two hundred sixty-two.
Shěn Héng’s younger brother Jùn, styled Shūshān,
had a good reputation,
but was naturally frugal and stingy.
Zhāng Wēn was to be sent to Shǔ and came to take leave of Jùn.
Jùn went inside for a long while,
then came out and said to Wēn,
“Just now I selected a bolt of cloth,
wishing to send it to you, but had nothing coarse enough.”
Wēn appreciated his open slight. Also seen in Lèi Jù eighty-five, Yùlǎn eight hundred twenty, Xùtánzhù four.
Again, he once passed the shore of Lake Tài,
and had his attendant fetch saltwater.
Later, he regretted having taken too much, and ordered it returned and reduced.
Soon after, he ashamedly said,
“This is my nature!” Guǎngjì one hundred fifteen-six.
Zhào Bógōng (Lèilín reads Wēng) was a large and fat man.
On a summer day, he lay drunk and sleeping.
His grandson, a few years old, climbed upon his belly and played,
and placed some plums (one source: eight or nine) in his navel.
After waking, he did not notice at all;
several days later, he felt pain.
The plums rotted, and juice came out,
forming a sore at the navel.
Fearing death, he ordered his wife and children to arrange family matters,
and tearfully told his household,
“My intestines have rotted; I am about to die.”
The next day, the plum pits fell out, and when questioned,
it was learned that the grandson had placed plums there.
Yùlǎn three hundred seventy-one and also nine hundred sixty-six, Yù Jí fourteen, Lèilín Záshuō ten.
In the time of Emperor Huán, someone resigned from the office of prefectural secretary,
and asked someone to compose a memorial.
That person could not compose it, and so said,
“In Liángguó, Gě Gǒngxiān is skilled in composition.
You may simply copy his, no need to trouble me.”
Following this advice, he copied the memorial,
but did not remove Gě Gǒng’s name.
The official was greatly shocked, gave no reply, and the matter was dropped.

For this, it became a saying of the day: “However skilled your memorial, best remove Gě Gǒng.” Yùlǎn four hundred ninety-six. (According to the Houhanshu, Gě Gǒng’s biography annotates: Gǒng was skilled at writing memorials. Some, requesting Gǒng to write for them, copied what he had written but forgot to omit his name, thereby submitting it with his name together. So the saying: “However skilled your memorial, best remove Gě Gǒng.” See Xiàolín, Yùlǎn for different versions.)
During the Han, Minister over the Masses Cuī Liè selected for service from Shàngdǎng
Bào Jiān as his secretary.
Bào Jiān was about to have an audience,
but feared he would fail the etiquette,
so asked those who had gone before about the ceremony.
One answered,
“Follow the guide’s prompts.”
When he went in, the prompter said, ‘Bow,’ and Jiān said, ‘Bow’;
the prompter said, ‘Take your seat,’ and Jiān said, ‘Take your seat.’
He then put his shoe on the seat,
and when about to leave, could not find his shoe.
The prompter said, “Your shoe is on your foot.”
Jiān also said, “My shoe is on my foot.”
Yùlǎn four hundred ninety-nine.
There was a man of Chǔ carrying a mountain rooster. A passerby asked, “What bird is that?”
The man, to deceive him, replied, “It is a fènghuáng!”
The passerby said, “I have heard of the fènghuáng for a long time and now truly behold it.
Are you selling it?”
“Indeed!” was the answer.
So the man paid a thousand in gold, but was refused; doubling the price, only then was it given.
He meant to present it to the King of Chǔ, but after a day the bird died.
The man did not begrudge the money, only lamented he could not present it.
The whole country heard the tale, believed it was a true fèng, and cherished it, all wishing to offer it.
Thus it reached the King of Chǔ.
The king, moved by their wish to offer him gifts,
summoned and generously rewarded them,
paying ten times the value of the purchased fèng. Guǎngjì four hundred sixty-one.
In Píngyuán, the Táoqiū family took a daughter of the Mòtái family from Bóhǎi as wife;
she was very beautiful and talented,
and they were respectful to each other.
After bearing a son, she returned to her family.
The mother, Lady Dīng, aged, came to see her, troubled in her heart.
The daughter, troubled in heart, returned and drove away her daughter-in-law.
At departure, the wife sought forgiveness.
The husband said, “When I saw the lady previously,
age and virtue had declined,
and she could not compare to her former self.
I also fear that when the new wife grows old, she too may become like this!
Therefore I sent her away,
truly for no other reason.”
Yùlǎn four hundred ninety-nine.
Someone served as an assistant in the Bà government, but was wholly lacking in understanding.
Whenever there were gatherings with music, he would join in;
being ashamed of his ignorance, when the performers played,
he would imitate others in praising and joining in harmony.
At that time, people made him host and had him summon the entertainers and guests.
When the entertainer guests had not yet arrived, he summoned the musical performers and asked about the music.
For each item, he recorded it below his handkerchief box.
There happened to be a prescription stored there; when all were present and a tune was requested,
he fetched the recorded item, but took the prescription by mistake,
and declared it was a list: “Three parts of aconite,
four parts of angelica.”
He said, “Just play ‘Aconite and Angelica’ to send off the guests.”
The whole gathering burst into laughter. Yùlǎn five hundred sixty-eight.
Someone from the south, visiting the capital, was warned:
“Whatever food you are given, just eat it—never ask its name!”
Upon arriving at his host’s home, he saw horse dung and ate it;
finding the smell foul, he stopped.
Entering, he saw cast-off old sandals by the road,
tried chewing them, but could not swallow at all.
He said to his companion, “Enough! What people say cannot all be believed.”
Later, visiting a nobleman, he was served food (one version: as a course)
and, seeing it, said, “You thing with a head (one version: old thing), let me not eat you.”
Yùlǎn six hundred ninety-eight, eight hundred fifty-one.
Someone making soup,
tasted it with a ladle; finding it lacking salt, he added some.
Tasting again, but from the same ladle, it still seemed lacking in salt.
In this way added several measures.
Yet still, it was not salty,
and he found it strange. Yùlǎn eight hundred sixty-one.
Jiǎ bought meat in the metropolis and went to the latrine,
hanging the meat outside.
Yǐ stole it,
but did not escape in time.
Jiǎ came out to look for his meat,
and Yǐ, pretending, held the meat in his mouth and said,
“You hung it outside—how could it not go missing?
If, like me, you held it in your mouth, it could never be lost.” Yùlǎn eight hundred sixty-two, Shū Chāo one hundred forty
five.
Yáo Biāo and Zhāng Wēn both traveled to Wǔchāng,
where they chanced upon Shěn Héng of Wúxīng at a riverbank, waiting for the wind.
Their provisions ran out, so they sent someone to borrow a hundred bushels of salt from Biāo.
Biāo, upright by nature,
received the letter but did not reply, and continued conversations with Wēn.
After a while, he ordered his aides:
“Pour a hundred bushels of salt into the river.”
He said to Wēn,
“Let it be known I am not stingy,
only careful with those to whom I give!” Guǎngjì one hundred sixty-five, Yùlǎn eight hundred sixty-five.
A man of Chǔ, living in poverty, read the Huáinánzǐ and came across
“The mantis waits for the cicada, holding a leaf to hide itself.”
So, under a tree, he looked up and sought leaves.
The mantis held the leaf to wait, and he picked it off; the leaves fell beneath the tree;
but there were already fallen leaves mixed below, and he could not distinguish them, so gathered several pecks to take home.
One by one he hid behind the leaves, asking his wife, “Can you see me?”
At first, his wife always replied, “I see you.”
After many days, she grew tired of it and, coaxing, said, “I don’t see you.”
Delighted, he carried the leaves to the market, and, in front of everyone, tried to obtain goods.
The officers arrested him and brought him to the county office.
There, he told the full story.
The officials laughed greatly and released him without punishment. Yùlǎn nine hundred forty-six.
In Han times, there was a man, old and without sons.
His family was rich, but frugal and miserly, wore poor clothing and ate coarse food,
rose early and worked until night;
managing his property, gathering and storing without end, yet never dared to use it himself.
When someone came to beg,
he unwillingly went inside to fetch ten coins, walked out from the hall,
at each step, reducing the amount, so that by the time he reached outside,
barely half remained, and with eyes closed he gave it to the beggar.
Soon after, he also cautioned,
“I have impoverished myself for your sake—never spread this,
or others will come imitating you!”
Before long the old man died; his property was confiscated by the government,
and his fortune filled the state treasury. Guǎngjì one hundred sixty-five.
There was a man named Jiǎ who wished to pay respects to the magistrate of the town. He asked those around him, "What does the magistrate like?"
Someone said to him, "He likes the commentary of Gōngyáng Fù."
Later, when he went in to see the magistrate, the magistrate asked, "What books do you read?"
He replied, "I study only the Gōngyáng Fù."
The magistrate tested him by asking, "Who killed Chén Tā?"
Jiǎ, after a long pause, answered, "In my life, I have truly never killed Chén Tā."
The magistrate noticed the error and jokingly said to him:
"Since you have not killed Chén Tā, then who did?"
At this Jiǎ was greatly frightened, and fled barefoot out the door.
Someone asked him the reason, and he loudly replied:
"When I saw the magistrate, he questioned me as though about a capital crime.
Hereafter I dare not go again; if I encounter a pardon, then I will come out." Miscellaneous Records 260
Jiǎ and Yǐ quarreled and fought;
Jiǎ bit off Yǐ’s nose.
The officials wished to judge the dispute;
Jiǎ claimed that Yǐ had bitten it off himself.
The official said, "People’s noses are high and their mouths are low; how could he bend to bite his own nose?"
Jiǎ said, "He stepped on a stool and bent over to bite it off." Miscellaneous Records 262
Jiǎ’s parents were alive, and he went away to study for three years before returning.
His maternal uncle asked what he had gained from his studies,
and also asked about being apart from his father for so long.
He then replied:
"The longing by the Wèi River surpasses even Qín Kāng’s."
Afterwards, his father scolded him:
"What benefit have you gained from your studies?"
He replied:
"As a child, I missed my father’s instruction in the courtyard, so my studies are without benefit." Miscellaneous Records 262
The people of Cāng wished to go together to mourn at a funeral, but none knew the proper rituals.
One said he knew the basics,
and told his companions, "Just follow my actions."
When they arrived at the mourning house,
the one with prior experience went first and bowed upon the mat.
The others, one by one, bumped their heads against each other’s backs;
the leader then kicked and cursed, saying, "Foolish fellow!"
The rest, thinking this was the proper ritual,
each in turn stepped on one another’s feet and said, "Foolish fellow!"
The last one came near the filial son;
he, too, stepped on the mourner and said, "Foolish fellow!" Miscellaneous Records 262
There was a foolish son-in-law whose father-in-law died;
his wife taught him how to perform the mourning rites.
On the way, he encountered a stream,
so he took off his socks to cross,
but left behind one sock.
Then, in the woods, he heard a dove calling, cooing, "gūgū, gūgū!"
He began to recite this to himself, and completely forgot the mourning rites.
When he arrived, he stood on one foot wearing a sock,
shrinking the barefoot one,
and only said, "gūgū, gūgū!"
All the mourners laughed.
He said again, "Don’t laugh, don’t laugh!
If you find my sock, please return it to me." Miscellaneous Records 262
There was a man in Lǔ carrying a long pole into the city gate.
At first he held it upright,
but could not get in;
when he held it horizontally,
he still could not get in;
he was at a loss for a solution.
Soon, there came an old man,
who said, "I am not a sage,
but I have seen many things in life.
Why not saw it in two and then enter?"
So the man did as suggested and sawed the pole in half. Miscellaneous Records 262
A man of Qí went to a man of Zhào to learn to play the sè.
But he spent his time adjusting the glue under the bridges and returned home,
three years passing without mastering even one tune.
The people of Qí thought it strange;
one who had come from Zhào
inquired and then understood the folly of that man. Miscellaneous Records 262
In Wú there was Hú Yōng,
a lustful man by nature.
He married Lady Zhāng,
whom he cherished so much he could not part from her.
Later, she died.
Yōng also passed away.
The family then kept the coffins in the backyard.
Three years later, they were to be properly buried.
It was seen that the earth of the tomb had turned into the shapes of two people,
always seen in embrace as if lying together.
People all vied to laugh at this.
Miscellaneous Records 389
There was a man of Hàn who traveled to Wú.
The people of Wú served him bamboo shoots.
He asked what this was.
They said it was bamboo!
He returned home and tried to cook his bamboo bed mat, but it would not become tender.
So he said to his wife:
"The people of Wú are truly deceitful,
tricking me like this!" Bamboo Shoots Records, Volume Eleven, Gǎnzhū Collection
